comments.thread: Which wines do you associate with the seasons? (r/wine/t1uc4j)
comments.author: NWisthebest
comments.text: For the most part it will be based on my seasonal cooking habits. In the summer, I eat more salad and do a large majority of cooking on the grill. Whereas in the winter I do more roasting and braising. Therefore I generally find myself drinking crisp whites (that are best served quite cold) and more hedonistic, younger reds (e.g., Zinfandel, Mourvedre, Tempranillo, etc.) in the summer, whereas in winter I lean more towards the richer whites (e.g., Chardonnay, Marsanne/Roussanne, etc.) and more complex reds (e.g., Pinot, Bordeaux, aged wines, etc.). Of course, when it all comes down to it, I drink whatever the hell I want, whenever the hell I want!

comments.thread: Why does wine always taste better at the winery? (r/wine/1skun0z)
comments.author: NapoleonTrilobite
comments.text: Wineries invest a lot of time and money into immersive tasting experiences. They guide you through tasting notes while you're at a beautiful venue and having great conversation with wines that have properly breathed in pristine stemware. Opening a bottle at home might not evoke that same magic. There so many itty bitty factors contributing to you drinking that first glass.

comments.thread: Why does wine always taste better at the winery? (r/wine/1skun0z)
comments.author: timbo415
comments.text: Theory I have: it's often the temperature of the wine. Too often at home people are drinking reds at room temp rather than trying to get them to ~57f before drinking.
